item.title: Modeling Transport and Mechanics in Anion Exchange Membranes to Optimize Continuous CO2 Separations
item.description: arXiv:2610.20812v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Water transport in charged polymer membranes is strongly influenced by hydration-dependent transport properties and polymer-network deformation. Under water-activity gradients, spatial variations in water concentration induce swelling and mechanical stresses, while the resulting deformation can influence water transport. Capturing this bidirectional interaction is important for predicting membrane behavior under nonuniform hydration conditions. This study develops a transient finite element model of water transport and mechanical deformation in a Fumasep FAA-3-50 anion exchange membrane. The framework incorporates concentration-dependent water diffusivity, hygroscopic swelling, and nonlinear viscoelastic polymer response. Uncoupled, one-way coupled, and fully coupled formulations are compared to distinguish the effects of hydration-dependent diffusivity and mechanical coupling. In the fully coupled model, local water concentration governs swelling and mechanical response, while deformation, evolving membrane geometry, and mechanical pressure feed back into water transport. Simulations predict spatially and temporally nonuniform swelling and deformation that track the evolving water-concentration field. Relative to the uncoupled concentration-dependent diffusion model, mechanical feedback alters the predicted transport response, although transport remains primarily diffusion-driven. The fully coupled model is validated against steady-state water-transport measurements across water-activity gradients and reproduces the experimentally observed hydration dependence, with strongest agreement at intermediate hydration levels. These results highlight the importance of coupled hydration, swelling, deformation, and transport processes in models of hydrated anion exchange membranes and provide a framework for evaluating membrane behavior in moisture-facilitated transport applications.
item.dc:creator: Samaneh Bayati, Jennifer Wade, Sara Sarbaz, Heidi Feigenbaum, Horacio Lopez-Marques, Winston Wang

item.title: Denser-than-crystalline disordered polydisperse ellipse packings
item.description: arXiv:2610.20953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: By employing SWAP Monte Carlo moves during slow Lubachevsky-Stillinger-like particle growth, we generate well-thermalized disordered jammed ellipse packings for a wide range of particle aspect ratios $\alpha$ and maximum/minimum particle-diameter ratios $\lambda$. For $\lambda > \lambda_{\rm xtal}(\alpha)$, the packings are denser than the perfect monodisperse ellipse crystal ($\phi_{\rm xtal}^{\rm mono} = \pi/2\sqrt{3} \simeq 0.9069$) despite lacking any obvious long-range structural order; we find that $\lambda_{\rm xtal}(\alpha)$ remains below $2.88$ over the range $1 \leq \alpha \leq 5$, and drops below $1.65$ for $\alpha \simeq 1.2$. These disordered $\phi > \phi_{\rm xtal}^{\rm mono}$ packings are the first of their kind reported for anisotropic particles. Multiscale analyses reveal that their characteristic structural motifs are strongly $\alpha$- and $\lambda$-dependent, but none of the examined metrics change sharply as the $\lambda = \lambda_{\rm xtal}(\alpha)$ boundary is crossed. For example, we find that packings with $\alpha \simeq 1.2$ and $\lambda \simeq \lambda_{\rm xtal}(\alpha)$ exhibit a fractionated-hexatic-plastic-polycrystalline structure that (like that of the recently-reported ideal disk glasses) can be exactly-isostatic, triangulated, and effectively-hyperuniform with respect to packing-fraction fluctuations. In contrast, even-denser packings with larger $\alpha$ and $\lambda$ have none of these properties.
item.dc:creator: Kinsley G. Trlak, Dewni S. de Silva, Salvatore Torquato, Robert S. Hoy

item.title: Universal Dynamic Scaling for Sub-Yield Aging and Over-Yield Rejuvenation in A Cyclically Driven Metallic Glass
item.description: arXiv:2610.21625v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whether sub-yield aging and over-yield rejuvenation in cyclically deformed amorphous solids share a common physical origin or arise from distinct microscopic mechanisms remains a fundamental yet unresolved debate. Using molecular dynamics simulations of a metallic glass, we resolve this duality by uncovering a unified dynamic clock that dictates energy landscape navigation across both regimes. We show that the transition between regimes reflects a fundamental shift in energy injection pathways: (i) In the over-yield regime, rejuvenation is driven as a first-order response to macroscopic plastic shear work derived from Herschel-Bulkley non-linear rheological scaling. (ii) In contrast, this macroscopic work scaling fails in the sub-yield regime, where early-stage energy landscape elevation and subsequent cyclic aging are instead governed by second-order localized elastic stress fluctuations acting as a mechanical catalyst and noise source, respectively. Intense high-rate agitation increases the escape probability from deeper potential energy minima, thereby suppressing the retention efficiency of structural relaxation. By identifying these localized fluctuations as the primary origin of rate-attenuated sub-yield relaxation, we establish an exact scaling identity relating the relaxation attenuation exponent to the stress fluctuation exponent. This work directly bridges non-linear rheology with stress fluctuation dynamics, providing a unified framework to predict and manipulate structural evolution in amorphous solids.
item.dc:creator: Nannan Ren, Hongfei Zhang, Rui Wan, Pengfei Guan, Limin Wang, Baoshuang Shang

item.title: Distribution Functions and Moments of Harmonically Trapped Inertial Run-and-Tumble Particles in a Shear-Thickening Medium
item.description: arXiv:2610.21650v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the dynamics of an athermal inertial active particle confined in a harmonic potential and moving through shear-thickening media in one dimension. The activity is modeled using a symmetric dichotomous noise of strength $\Sigma$ and flipping rate $\lambda$, which mimics a run-and-tumble particle. The shear-thickening response of the medium is incorporated through a velocity-dependent viscous force of the form $g(v) \sim \tan(v)$. Starting from the Fokker-Planck equations corresponding to the particle's dynamics, we numerically compute the time-dependent joint probability density function $f(x,v,t)$ using a finite-volume upwind scheme. Next, we numerically solve the particle's equations of motion to obtain the steady-state position $P_s(x)$ and velocity $W_s(v)$ distributions and compare them with the marginal distributions obtained from $f(x,v,t)$ at sufficiently large $t$. The two approaches show excellent agreement. Both $P_s(x)$ and $W_s(v)$ exhibit several intriguing transitions as $\lambda$ is varied, and they eventually approach Gaussian-like profiles at sufficiently large $\lambda$. Our study of the time-dependent position-velocity correlation, $\langle xv \rangle(t)$, shows that larger values of $\lambda$ lead to faster relaxation to the steady state when all other parameters are held constant.
item.dc:creator: Subhanker Howlader, Prasenjit Das

item.title: Spatiotemporally correlated activity regulation of random-organizing hyperuniform states
item.description: arXiv:2610.21769v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Center-of-mass (COM) conservation has been widely accepted as an important mechanism for generating nonequilibrium dynamic hyperuniform states with vanishing long-wavelength density fluctuations, but whether it is sufficient for hyperuniformity remains unclear. Here, using particle simulations and a linear fluctuating theory, we show that spatiotemporally correlated activity regulation can destroy hyperuniformity while preserving COM conservation. We construct a binary mixture in which the local density of independently evolving driver particles regulates the activity of regulated particles following COM-conserving biased random organization. This counterexample demonstrates that hyperuniformity depends on the spatial and temporal correlations of activity as well as the conservation laws governing particle displacements. Our findings clarify the limits of COM conservation as a route to hyperuniformity and highlight the importance of controlling activity correlations in the design of nonequilibrium multihyperuniform mixtures.
item.dc:creator: Yuhan Peng, Yusheng Lei, Ran Ni

item.title: Drying-Induced Size Segregation and Stratification in Colloidal Droplets across Binary, Ternary, and Polydisperse Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.21816v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study evaporation-induced size segregation and stratification in binary, ternary, and polydisperse mixtures of colloidal particles within a drying droplet using Brownian dynamics (BD) simulations. We show that drying-induced stratification can occur in all three types of mixtures, with larger particles preferentially accumulating in the droplet interior and smaller particles near the droplet surface. In binary mixtures, size segregation becomes more pronounced as the Peclet number and the size difference between particles increase, and as the relative volume fraction of large particles and the initial particle concentration decrease. In ternary mixtures, three distinct layers form when the Peclet number is sufficiently high and the intermediate particle size is suitably selected. Under the conditions studied, increasing the fraction of intermediate-sized particles can also enhance separation between the small and large particles. These results are in qualitative agreement with previous studies of drying planar films. Extending the analysis to polydisperse systems, we find that the average particle size decreases with increasing radial distance under stratifying conditions. Furthermore, higher Peclet numbers and particle-size distributions with more particles at both size extremes lead to steeper radial gradients in particle size. Additionally, we use multi-particle collision dynamics (MPCD) simulations to assess the role of hydrodynamic interactions. BD simulations predict stronger stratification than MPCD simulations, although stratification persists in the MPCD simulations. Our results thus demonstrate that droplet-confined drying offers a simple and versatile strategy for engineering radial composition and size gradients in colloidal assemblies, thereby offering new opportunities for the controlled fabrication of hierarchically structured supraparticles.
item.dc:creator: Zhoaxuan Liu, Marjolein Dijkstra

item.title: From Action Principle to Stochastic Thermodynamics of Elastic and Viscous Active Matter
item.description: arXiv:2610.21835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by the complex material properties of living matter, we derive a framework of stochastic thermo- and elastodynamics for active materials from the classical principle of least action and the Rayleighian formalism for external forces. Our approach couples the local barycentric collective coordinate and the streaming velocity as the canonical conjugate pair, which unifies various descriptions of elastic and viscous soft matter, including Helfrich theory for lipid membranes, linear and nonlinear elasticity of thin shells and deformable droplets, as well as hydrodynamics of active and passive fluids. The Lagrangian mechanics of collective field variables permits direct applications of the results and theorems from statistical mechanics to existing models of complex soft and living matter. To illustrate the potential applications of stochastic elastodynamics in biology, we derive and simulate a boundary-driven deformation model of an elastic cell nucleus in the presence of fluctuations.
item.dc:creator: Valentina Barletta, Michele Lupini, Ian D. Estabrook, Laeschkir W\"urthner, Isabella R. Graf, Caren Norden, Lamberto Rondoni, Anna Erzberger, Roman Belousov

item.title: Phase coexistence and nucleation of aging condensates
item.description: arXiv:2610.21917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Biomolecular condensates form by phase separation and often age over time by transitioning from liquid-like droplets to solid-like states. To capture the fundamental behavior of aging condensates, we connect the Flory-Huggins model of phase separation with the trap model of aging dynamics. This combined model yields a rich phase diagram, including a regime of metastable coexisting liquids. Interestingly, the dense metastable liquid serves as an intermediate state in the nucleation pathway of the glass, which thus nucleates in two steps. Our results are generic, since they follow from a basic free-energy structure, providing a unified foundation for describing the thermodynamics and kinetics of aging biomolecular condensates.
item.dc:creator: Yicheng Qiang, Chengjie Luo, David Zwicker

item.title: PANDA-D: Interface-free determination of two dynamic contact angles
item.description: arXiv:2610.21996v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Contact angles are central descriptors of wetting and capillary behavior at solid--fluid interfaces. Dynamic contact angles in molecular simulations are commonly extracted from two-dimensional liquid--vapor contours and near-wall tangent fits. We introduce PANDA-D, an extension of Predicting Angle from Nanoscale Density Analysis (PANDA) that determines both contact angles of a driven liquid roll without extracting an interface. The density profile measures occupied layer width but does not identify which meniscus is advancing. The method resolves this ambiguity by jointly fitting density and the layerwise center-of-mass displacement relative to the roll. A circular-meniscus model maps these profiles to receding and advancing angles and an effective near-wall offset. On synthetic rolls with prescribed angles, the reconstruction error is $0.29^\circ$ root-mean-square. We then analyze force-driven Lennard--Jones rolls between crystalline walls. Joint fits reproduce both measured profiles, whereas density-only fits can match density while assigning incorrect asymmetry. The resulting angles agree with independently determined circle-fit angles to $0.84^\circ$ root-mean-square. Across four wall--fluid attractions, the receding angle decreases and the advancing angle increases with force, approximately linearly over the studied ranges. By eliminating contour thresholds and near-wall tangent extrapolation from the primary estimate, the two-profile approach enables reproducible, automated angle analysis across molecular trajectories.
item.dc:creator: Georgii K. Vandyshev, Grigorii S. Gorkaev, Nikolay D. Kondratyuk, Kirill M. Gerke, Ilia V. Kopanichuk

item.title: Platelet-driven contraction enlarges accessible space in layered fibrin networks without uniformly accelerating particle escape
item.description: arXiv:2610.20762v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Platelet traction contracts fibrin networks, yet whether contraction promotes or hinders the escape of suspended particles is unclear. We coupled an overdamped Langevin model of platelet--fibrin mechanics to Brownian transport of finite-size tracers through frozen network states. Nine mechanical replicas were evolved at four filopodial traction baselines (0--8.8\,nN), stacked into 5-$\mu$m-thick domains of 50 layers and probed at 0--15\,s with 0.5-$\mu$m tracers (29,952 trajectories, 100\,s observation). Benchmarked against experimental clot-contraction kinetics, the simulated contraction is post-lag, within one order of magnitude of experimental rates and corresponds to the onset of the contraction phase. Relative to the matched zero-baseline control, every active-baseline state showed greater projected contraction and a larger tracer-accessible volume ($+9.3\%$ to $+27.6\%$; exact sign test $p=0.0039$ per condition). At 15\,s, mean survival at 100\,s fell from 27.3\% to 14.3\% and the restricted mean exit time from 56.5 to 44.0\,s between the lowest and highest baseline, and all nine replicas shortened residence at 8.8\,nN. At lower baselines, responses differed among replicas, and nearly all retained tracers with a classified start were connected to an exit. Contraction therefore enlarges accessible space without uniformly accelerating escape, separating geometric accommodation from transport kinetics.
item.dc:creator: Juan P. Staforelli-Vivanco, Paolo Teppa Gutierrez

item.title: Vision-Guided Closed-Loop Autonomous Navigation of Light-Driven Janus Microbots
item.description: arXiv:2610.21222v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Artificial microbots capable of precise and autonomous navigation could provide versatile platforms for microscale transport, manipulation, and task execution in complex environments. However, reliable navigation becomes increasingly challenging at the micrometre scale, particularly when the surrounding environment changes dynamically. Here, we develop a vision-guided closed-loop navigation framework for light-driven cube-shaped hematite/TiO2 Janus microbots with a characteristic size of approximately 3 {\mu}m. Real-time visual localization using a custom-trained YOLOv11 object-detection model is integrated with discretized waypoint-based magnetic steering to enable precise navigation along complex prescribed trajectories, with more than 90% of the measured trajectory deviations remaining below 6 {\mu}m across the tested path geometries. The framework further enables arbitrary user-defined free-hand trajectories and autonomous navigation through a physically confined maze. In dynamically changing environments, A* path planning enables real-time path replanning while avoiding multiple independently swimming 5 {\mu}m spherical Janus micromotors. Finally, the microbot selectively captures multiple cargo particles and autonomously transports and delivers them to a predefined location while simultaneously avoiding dynamic obstacles. These results establish an integrated platform combining programmable trajectory control, autonomous path planning, real-time environmental adaptation, and task execution within a single light-driven Janus microbot system.
item.dc:creator: Kanhu Charan Andia, Harsh Prashant Katole, Parth Nitinkumar Bhosale, Hemant Kumar, Dhruv Pratap Singh

item.title: Dynamic Coarse-Graining of Linear and Non-Linear Systems: Mori-Zwanzig Formalism and Beyond
item.description: arXiv:2307.08143v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: To investigate the impact of non-linear interactions on dynamic coarse graining, we study a simplified model system, featuring a tracer particle in a complex environment. Using a projection operator formalism and computer simulations, we systematically derive generalized Langevin equations (GLEs) describing the dynamics of this particle. We compare different kinds of linear and non-linear coarse-graining procedures to understand how non-linearities enter reconstructed generalized Langevin equations and how they influence the coarse-grained dynamics. For non-linear external potentials, we show analytically and numerically that the non-Gaussian parameter and the incoherent intermediate scattering function will not be correctly reproduced by the GLE if a linear projection is applied. This, however, can be overcome by using non-linear projection operators. We also study anharmonic coupling between the tracer and the environment and demonstrate that the reconstructed memory kernel develops an additional trap-dependent contribution. Our study highlights some open challenges and possible solutions in dynamic coarse graining.
item.dc:creator: Bernd Jung, Gerhard Jung

item.title: Dirac Representation for Lattice Spin Operators: Spin-$1/2$ and Spin-$1$ cases
item.description: arXiv:2504.11917v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a quantum representation of lattice spin operators (LSOs) by mapping quantum spins to their classical analogues for spin values $S=1/2$ and $S=1$. The resulting Dirac (bra--ket) forms are derived from the structure of binary and ternary digit distributions in non-negative integers. \color{blue} The construction requires only an enumeration of the lattice sites and is therefore independent on the spatial dimension and lattice geometry. \color{black} Analytical expressions for extracting the $j$th bit or trit of an integer without performing an explicit binary or ternary decomposition are obtained. \color{blue}As an application of the representation, \color{black} we analyze the one-dimensional spin-$1/2$ {XXZ} Heisenberg model with open boundaries in a magnetic field in both absence (uniform magnetic field) and presence of disorder (random magnetic field). In the absence of disorder (clean system), we demonstrate that the corresponding eigenvalue problem can be reduced to a tight-binding problem on a graph. For the isotropic case, this is solved analytically without resorting to any spinless transformation or the Bethe Ansatz. In the presence of disorder, a convergent perturbation theory is elaborated. Our analytical results are benchmarked against exact diagonalization for systems up to $K\leq 18$ spins. These computations exploit the global $U(1)$ symmetry to block-diagonalize the Hamiltonian and the spin-inversion symmetry to further decompose the zero-magnetization sector. Quantitative agreement between analytical and numerical results is observed.
item.dc:creator: Maseim Bassis Kenmoe

item.title: Density and shape govern the dynamical self-organization of active matter on a closed surface
item.description: arXiv:2603.23735v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Morphogenesis emerges from dynamic feedback among geometry, mechanics, and chemistry; however, disentangling these contributions in living systems remains challenging. Here, we focus on the interplay between geometry and mechanics by developing a minimal in vitro model in which purified microtubules and kinesin motor clusters self-organize into a two-dimensional active nematic cortex at the surface of spherical water-in-oil droplets. The spherical geometry enforces a total topological charge of +2, here realized by four +1/2 defects whose trajectories reveal robust, self-sustained oscillations. Using full-surface reconstructions, we show that the collective dynamics of the defects lead to a periodic switching between planar and tetrahedral arrangements through alternating coiling and hemisphere-crossing phases. By tuning microtubule density, the system spans a continuum from a classic defect-dominated active nematic to a regime resembling an extensile filament confined to a curved surface, where low density is associated with increased trajectory variability and direction reversals. Geometric perturbations introduced through controlled squeezing redistribute curvature and induce the nucleation of additional defects, thereby reorganizing the entire topological landscape while preserving total charge. Together, these results show that periodic morphogenetic-like cycles, defect topology, and material organization can arise solely from the interplay of activity, density, and curvature. This reconstituted system provides a versatile platform for elucidating the coupling between mechanics and geometry underlying shape formation in active biological matter.
item.dc:creator: Romain Leroux, Andre Estevez-Torres, Raphael Voituriez, Ananyo Maitra, Nicolas Lobato-Dauzier, Jean-Christophe Galas

item.title: Exact dynamics and dimensional effects in torque-driven trapped active Brownian particles
item.description: arXiv:2603.26967v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The interplay of chirality, self-propulsion, and confinement generates pronounced non-equilibrium fluctuations, with higher-order moments encoding the shape of the position distribution. We present an exact analytical framework, based on the Laplace transform of the Fokker-Planck equation, for the transient dynamics of a chiral active Brownian particle in a harmonic trap in two and three dimensions. Closed-form expressions for time-dependent moments up to fourth order allow a full characterization of the excess kurtosis across transient and steady-state regimes. In two dimensions, the excess kurtosis exhibits damped oscillations with multiple re-entrant crossovers, evolving from negative values, indicative of off-centered ring-like distributions, to small positive values characteristic of near-Gaussian distributions with a weak tail enhancement; increasing trap stiffness progressively suppresses this oscillatory response. In three dimensions, the excess kurtosis of a torque-driven active Brownian particle stays negative, reflecting robust non-Gaussian fluctuations with half-ring- to band-like position distributions in the plane defined by the torque axis. These results reveal how chirality, propulsion, confinement, and dimensionality jointly shape transient dynamics and provide experimentally accessible signatures of confined chiral active motion.
item.dc:creator: Anweshika Pattanayak, Amir Shee, Abhishek Chaudhuri, Debasish Chaudhuri

item.title: Mechanistic insights into the spatial organization of RNA polymerase proteins and the chromosome in E. coli cells
item.description: arXiv:2604.02838v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Along the bacterial chromosome, regions called rrn operons contain genes that are transcribed into ribosomal RNA. These operons are among the most transcriptionally active sites in the genome. It has been observed in E. coli that RNA polymerase (RNAP), while binding to these genetic loci along the chromosome during transcription, forms dense clusters, leading to spatial colocalization of the operons within the cell. Recent experimental evidence suggests that liquid-liquid phase separation contributes to the formation of RNAP clusters, with the antitermination factor NusA playing a key role. We present a simulation model to investigate the mechanisms underlying the formation of these biomolecular condensates. We propose that mutual attraction between NusA proteins, which exhibit a miscibility gap at higher concentrations, drives condensate formation via a polymer-assisted condensation pathway, and we demonstrate how these condensates promote the colocalization of rrn operons. Our results reconcile seemingly disparate experimental observations of chromosomal organization reported in fluorescence-based imaging and Hi-C experiments.
item.dc:creator: Debarshi Mitra, Jens-Uwe Sommer

item.title: Various phases of active matter emerging from bacteria and their implications
item.description: arXiv:2604.13575v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this perspective article, we discuss bacterial populations as a model system of active matter. It allows for the exploration and characterization of various phases of active matter and brings rich implications for both physics and biology. Specifically, we focus on active gas, active liquid, active glass and active liquid crystal states observed in bacterial populations and describe how these differ from their thermal counterparts. A few future directions are also discussed that will deepen the physical interest in active matter as a new type of material, with its implications for several life phenomena observed in bacterial populations and other biological systems.
item.dc:creator: Kazumasa A. Takeuchi, Daiki Nishiguchi

item.title: Limits of the Non-Linear Generalized Langevin Equation: Cross-Correlations, Irreversibility and Desynchronization
item.description: arXiv:2605.31297v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The generalized Langevin equation (GLE) is widely used to model complex soft-matter systems, including biomolecular dynamics, by incorporating memory effects and colored noise into coarse-grained descriptions. However, recent results suggest that combining memory with non-linear forces, ubiquitous in soft matter, introduces fundamental analytical inconsistencies. Here, using a simplified model, we investigate the practical numerical consequences of these analytical results. We show that non-linear forces generate cross-correlations with the noise, modifying the fluctuation-dissipation theorem and rendering the noise position-dependent and irreversible. This implies that the commonly assumed reversible Gaussian noise in GLE simulations fails to capture essential features of the microscopic fluctuations. For weak non-linearities, these issues can be partially resolved either by using an iterative optimization of memory or by using microscopically consistent noise, which unexpectedly synchronizes GLE trajectories with the underlying microscopic dynamics. For stronger non-linearities like high barriers or shoulders in the external potential, however, iterative reconstruction fails and we observe desynchronization, indicating that the non-linear GLE no longer correctly reproduces the microscopic dynamics. Our results show in which situations non-linear GLEs can be accurately applied and when they fail, thus providing practical guidance for their application to coarse-grain soft-matter systems.
item.dc:creator: Bernd Jung, Gerhard Jung

item.title: Controlling Turbulent Flows in Compressible Active Liquid Crystals
item.description: arXiv:2607.24927v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Motivated by experiments on light-patterned, quasi-2D active suspensions that exhibit large density variations, we develop a continuum theory of compressible active nematics--suspensions of apolar rods whose orientation is invariant under $\pi$ rotations. Under spatially patterned activity, the extensile isotropic active pressure expels material from high-activity regions and accumulates it in low-activity ones; an exactly solvable scalar reduction shows that the resulting density contrast is governed by a single dimensionless parameter, linear in the compressibility. Using compressibility as a tuning knob, we then steer active turbulence from high- to low-activity regions and, at sharp activity interfaces, stabilize an analytically tractable dynamical steady state: a one-dimensional chain of vortices held by soft, activity-induced confinement. Our results establish compressibility as a control parameter for density variations and turbulent flow in active nematic suspensions.
item.dc:creator: Dimitrios Krommydas, Paarth Gulati, Aparna Baskaran, M. Cristina Marchetti

item.title: Experimental Observation of Mesoscopic Dynamic Fluctuations in Water-Alcohol Mixtures
item.description: arXiv:2608.30098v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We applied a dynamic fluctuation measurement method to liquid water-methanol mixtures over a wide range of compositions and temperatures. This method, which we developed in recent years, combines ultrasonic and inelastic X-ray scattering techniques to detect mesoscopic-level fluctuations - that is, the degree of heterogeneity - in liquids using sound waves. As a result, it was found that dynamic fluctuations exist across a wide range of compositions and temperatures, including pure substances (water and methanol). Furthermore, in the low-methanol composition range (approximately 20% mol or less), the strength of dynamic fluctuation increased toward lower compositions and lower temperatures, suggesting that the origin of the fluctuation lies in the low temperature (supercooled) region of water alone. Conversely, this indicates that in the range below 20% methanol, fluctuations in water alone are dominant rather than the mixed effects of water and methanol. We performed similar dynamic fluctuation measurements on water-ethanol and water-glycerol mixtures at room temperature. We found that dynamic fluctuations exist universally across the entire composition range, and confirmed an increase in the strength of dynamic fluctuations toward lower compositions in the regions approximately below 15% and below 20%, respectively. This revealed that the phenomenon is not unique to methanol systems but is a common behavior shared by water-alcohol mixtures. It has long been known that water-alcohol mixtures exhibit various thermodynamic anomalies, but the mechanisms behind them have not yet been fully elucidated. The present results are expected to provide a new direction for discussion on this issue.
item.dc:creator: Yukio Kajihara, Nanako Shibata, Masanori Inui

item.title: Domain of Applicability of the Distorted Wave Born Approximation (DWBA): A Critical Analysis for X-ray and Visible-Light Interface Scattering
item.description: arXiv:2610.14054v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Distorted Wave Born Approximation (DWBA) is established for X-ray interface scattering, yet its domain of applicability has never been stated explicitly. The DWBA implicitly rests on the small refractive index deviation (SRID) condition - satisfied by X-rays ($|n-1| \sim 10^{-6}$) but violated by visible light ($|n-1| \sim 0.5$). The DWBA mixes microscopic and macroscopic Maxwell equations, whereas a rigorous optical theory must be built on the macroscopic Maxwell equations and constitutive relations. Rigorous alternatives for two specific inconsistencies in the standard DWBA are discussed. The Extended Transfer Matrix Approach (ETMA) for visible-light interface scattering is outlined.
item.dc:creator: Reinhard Sigel

item.title: Transient compressible flow in a compliant viscoelastic tube
item.description: arXiv:2007.03077v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Motivated by problems arising in the pneumatic actuation of controllers for micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS), labs-on-a-chip or biomimetic soft robots, and the study of microrheology of both gases and soft solids, we analyze the transient fluid--structure interaction (FSIs) between a viscoelastic tube conveying compressible flow at low Reynolds number. We express the density of the fluid as a linear function of the pressure, and we use the lubrication approximation to further simplify the fluid dynamics problem. On the other hand, the structural mechanics is governed by a modified Donnell shell theory accounting for Kelvin--Voigt-type linearly viscoelastic mechanical response. The fluid and structural mechanics problems are coupled through the tube's radial deformation and the hydrodynamic pressure. For small compressibility numbers and weak coupling, the equations are solved analytically via a perturbation expansion. Three illustrative problems are analyzed. First, we obtain exact (but implicit) solutions for the pressure for steady flow conditions. Second, we solve the transient problem of impulsive pressurization of the tube's inlet. Third, we analyze the transient response to an oscillatory inlet pressure. We show that an oscillatory inlet pressure leads to acoustic streaming in the tube, attributed to the nonlinear pressure gradient induced by the interplay of FSI and compressibility. Furthermore, we demonstrate an enhancement in the volumetric flow rate due to FSI coupling. The hydrodynamic pressure oscillations are shown to exhibit a low-pass frequency response (when averaging over the period of oscillations), while the frequency response of the tube deformation is similar to that of a band-pass filter.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Physics of Fluids 32, 112014 (2020); Erratum, Phys. Fluids 38, 109902 (2026)
item.dc:creator: Vishal Anand, Ivan C. Christov

item.title: Divergence of Light Wave Amplitudes in an Interface Layer at Critical Conditions
item.description: arXiv:2606.16841v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The amplitudes of light modes in a homogeneous interface layer are investigated around the critical conditions (CC) in a total reflection geometry. CC occur when the normal wave vector vanishes; the resulting divergence upon variation of the angle of incidence is characterized by a critical exponent -0.5. Absorption replaces the divergence with a finite peak whose width and height are derived analytically. The high relevance of the amplification for Evanescent Wave Dynamic Light Scattering (EWDLS) is demonstrated using published experimental data. The relation to surface plasmon resonance (SPR) is briefly discussed. An outlook connects the amplitude divergence to a critical analysis of the Distorted Wave Born Approximation (DWBA) presented in a companion paper.
item.dc:creator: Reinhard Eduard Sigel
